title: Effect of Thermal, Acoustic and Air Quality Perception Interactions on the Comfort and Satisfaction of People in Office Buildings
research_question: Is there a cross-modal effect of thermal, acoustic and air quality perception on occupants' comfort? How does indoor environmental quality affect thermal perception?

participants.description: Stage 1: 26 participants; Stage 2: 1079 responses from 116 individual participants; Stage 3: 12 participants. All were administrative staff, academic staff, and postgraduate researchers working in mixed-mode university office buildings at the University of Southampton, UK.
participants.recruitment: Participants consented to participate in questionnaire surveys.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three mixed-mode university office buildings (B1, B2, B3) at the University of Southampton, UK, with open plan and cellular office spaces. Environmental conditions (sound pressure levels, air temperature, relative humidity) were monitored concurrently with surveys in Stage 3.

mechanisms: The feeling of "stuffiness" (associated with bad air quality and warm thermal sensation) is often attributed to low air movement, high relative humidity, and high carbon dioxide concentration.
As noise levels increase, participants may become less sensitive to interruption disturbances.
moderators: Room occupancy type (individual office vs. open plan/shared office)
Air quality perception (ASV) moderates the effect of operative temperature (Top) on thermal sensation (TSV).
Air quality perception (ASV) moderates the effect of sound pressure levels (SPL30) on thermal sensation (TSV).
implementation_implications: Open plan office designs should include provisions for noise control.
Air quality in office buildings will play an important role in future building design and services systems.
Longitudinal, POE-comfort mixed surveys are useful tools for investigating building design and environmental factors on occupants' comfort and behaviour.
A trans-modal comfort approach could be used to develop adaptive, reactive, and dynamic building systems that respond to occupant-specific zonal conditions, preferences, and personalized controls.

limitations: Results may not be generalizable to non-university office buildings.
Differences between POE and 'right-here-right-now' surveys might limit direct comparison of results.
Variation in sample size and survey duration across stages might introduce seasonal effects on questionnaire results.
Impact of different data collection methods on sample size and response quality needs further examination.
Findings may only apply to buildings with similar mixed-mode ventilation characteristics and adaptive opportunities.
Generalization is restricted by the sample size and participant characteristics (highly educated, environmentally aware, energy-saving attitudes, working in academic disciplines).

paper_metadata.title: Effect of Thermal, Acoustic and Air Quality Perception Interactions on the Comfort and Satisfaction of People in Office Buildings
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effect of Thermal, Acoustic and Air Quality Perception Interactions on the Comfort and Satisfaction of People in Office Buildings
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Current research on human comfort has identified a gap in the investigation of multi-domain perception interactions. There is a lack of understanding the interrelationships of different physio-socio-psychological factors and the manifestation of their contextual interactions into cross-modal comfort perception. In that direction, this study used data from a post occupancy evaluation survey (n = 26), two longitudinal comfort studies (n = 1079 and n = 52) and concurrent measurements of indoor environmental quality factors (one building) to assess the effect of thermal, acoustic and air quality perception interactions on comfort and satisfaction of occupants in three mixed-mode university office buildings. The study concluded that thermal sensation (TSV) is associated with both air quality (ASV) and noise perception (NSV). The crossed effect of the interaction of air quality and noise perception on thermal sensation was not evident. The key finding was the significant correlation of operative temperature (Top) with TSV as expected, but also with noise perception and overall acoustic comfort. Regarding the crossed main effects on thermal sensation, a significant effect was found for the interactions of (1) Top and (2) sound pressure levels (SPL30) with air quality perception respectively. Most importantly, this study has highlighted the importance of air quality perception in achieving occupants’ comfort and satisfaction with office space.

crossref_abstract: Current research on human comfort has identified a gap in the investigation of multi-domain perception interactions. There is a lack of understanding the interrelationships of different physio-socio-psychological factors and the manifestation of their contextual interactions into cross-modal comfort perception. In that direction, this study used data from a post occupancy evaluation survey (n = 26), two longitudinal comfort studies (n = 1079 and n = 52) and concurrent measurements of indoor environmental quality factors (one building) to assess the effect of thermal, acoustic and air quality perception interactions on comfort and satisfaction of occupants in three mixed-mode university office buildings. The study concluded that thermal sensation (TSV) is associated with both air quality (ASV) and noise perception (NSV). The key finding was the significant correlation of operative temperature (Top) with TSV as expected, but also with noise perception and overall acoustic comfort. Regarding the crossed main effects on thermal sensation, a significant effect was found for the interactions of (1) Top and (2) sound pressure levels (SPL30) with air quality perception respectively. Most importantly, this study has highlighted the importance of air quality perception in achieving occupants’ comfort and satisfaction with office space.

environmental_features: Air quality (CO2 concentration, perceived stuffiness/freshness, ventilation)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: People adapt to their thermal environment over time, influencing their comfort perceptions and expectations.

mechanism_chain.description: Perceptions of thermal, acoustic, and air quality conditions interact to influence overall comfort and satisfaction, where multiple stressors can have a synergistic negative impact.
